name: Psoralen (PUVA, bergamot oil tanning)
lead: Psoralen is the parent compound of the linear furanocoumarins, plant-derived photosensitizing chemicals that bind DNA when exposed to UVA light. They occur in figs, celery, parsley, citrus fruit and, in the form of bergapten and bergamottin, in bergamot oil [1].

Medically, psoralen plus UVA (PUVA) is used to treat psoriasis, vitiligo and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma [1][2]. In tanning culture, psoralen-containing products, including bergamot oil, were used as tanning activators intended to deepen pigmentation after sun exposure, so that a darker tan appeared faster. Psoralen-based tanning activators were used in sun products until 1996, when they were banned after being found photocarcinogenic [1][3]. In vitiligo, the same pigment-stimulating action is used to re-colour pale patches, which links the compound to skin-tone evening as well as tanning [2].

Psoralens are phototoxic: some people suffered severe skin loss after sunbathing with products containing them [1]. Long-term PUVA treatment is associated with higher skin cancer rates, including squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma [1][2][4].

Research on the compound spans dermatology trials, a long-running cohort study of PUVA-treated psoriasis patients, and molecular biology, where its DNA-crosslinking property is used as a laboratory tool [4][5].

paras: With UVA light, psoralen forms monoadducts and interstrand cross-links with thymine bases in DNA, which can induce apoptosis [1]. This photochemistry is also exploited in molecular biology to study DNA and RNA structure [5]. In skin, the damage response stimulates melanocytes, which is why psoralen plus light darkens skin.

Wikipedia describes psoralen as the parent of the linear furanocoumarins and notes that its derivatives, such as 8-methoxypsoralen (methoxsalen), 5-methoxypsoralen (bergapten) and trimethylpsoralen, differ in potency. [1] A 2020 paper describes work on psoralen derivatives with enhanced potency for photochemotherapy. [10] The same DNA-binding property is used in laboratories to map RNA duplexes and DNA structure in living cells. [5]

Bergamot essential oil comes from the peel of Citrus bergamia, grown mainly in the Reggio di Calabria province of Italy, with smaller amounts in southern France, the Ivory Coast and Turkey; about 100 oranges yield roughly 85 grams of oil. [9] The oil is widely used in perfumery and flavours Earl Grey tea. [9]

Wikipedia attributes the oil's phototoxicity mainly to bergapten, with possible contributions from citropten, bergamottin, geranial and neral, and notes that guinea-pig patch tests showed a concentration-dependent phototoxic reaction; it says skin use can increase photosensitivity. [9] Phototoxic furanocoumarins also occur in other citrus and in plants such as rue and figs, which is why contact with lime juice or celery followed by sun can cause phytophotodermatitis. [12][9]

PUVA treats vitiligo, psoriasis, eczema, graft-versus-host disease, mycosis fungoides and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, with psoralen given orally, topically or in baths before UVA exposure [2]. Ancient Egyptian use of Ammi majus juice plus sunlight on vitiligo is described, and modern PUVA began in 1940s Cairo with methoxsalen [2]. Narrowband UVB is now more commonly used for vitiligo [2].

Psoralen-induced phytophotodermatitis, a skin reaction to plant furocoumarins and UVA, has been reviewed as a diagnostic and management topic in dermatology, with psoralen named as the most common phototoxic furocoumarin. [12]

Bergamot oil contains psoralens and was used in cosmetic tanning preparations. Psoralen-containing tanning activators were sold in sunscreens until 1996, and in 1980 and 1981 studies linked 5-methoxypsoralen, a tanning additive, to lethal and mutagenic effects and tumours in mice [1]. Health authorities banned the activators in July 1996 [3].

Wikipedia's bergamot article states that the photocarcinogenicity of psoralen was known from 1959 yet psoralen-containing tanning accelerators and sunscreens remained in use until 1995, and links their use to cases of melanoma. [9] This history is cited in discussions of how tanning products were regulated. [1][3]
No studies were found of psoralen or bergamot oil as a cosmetic tanning aid. Studies of medical PUVA exist.

The PUVA Follow-Up Study, a cohort of psoriasis patients treated with methoxsalen and UVA, reported an elevated risk of malignant melanoma [4]. A prospective study of 23 patients with symmetrical vitiligo compared calcipotriol ointment plus PUVA on one side of the body with PUVA alone on the other; at the 15th session 69 percent had minimal to moderate improvement on the calcipotriol side versus 52 percent on the PUVA-only side, and the authors reported good tolerance [13]. A randomized study compared medium-dose UVA1 with topical PUVA in acral vitiligo [11].

Registered trials include a 2026 comparison of PUVA with tofacitinib in generalized vitiligo (NCT07055529) and a 2013 study of topical PUVA versus narrowband UVB for recalcitrant hand dermatoses (NCT01792245). [6][7] A 2018 review of phototherapy and a 2020 review of phototherapy for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma describe PUVA among the established light-based treatments. [8][15]

Short-term effects include nausea, vomiting, redness, itching, dry skin and pain from phototoxic nerve damage [1]. Long-term oral PUVA is associated with higher skin cancer rates, notably squamous cell carcinoma [2]. Psoralens are described as photocarcinogenic [1].

Psoralen-based tanning activators sold in sun products until 1996 were banned by health authorities, and the history is a standard example of a tanning product withdrawn on safety grounds. [1][3] Today psoralen is encountered mostly in medical phototherapy, in perfumery and food discussions of bergamot, and as a cause of phytophotodermatitis after contact with citrus or other plants. [2][12][9]

card.summary: A plant-derived photosensitizer that supercharges tanning under UVA; used medically as PUVA, but its tanning use was banned for phototoxic and cancer concerns.
card.note: Phototoxic and photocarcinogenic; tanning activators containing it were withdrawn in 1996.

quick.overview:
Psoralens are light-sensitizing compounds found in plants such as figs, celery and citrus, including bergamot oil. With UVA light they darken skin, and doctors use them in PUVA therapy for conditions like vitiligo and psoriasis.

Some tanning products once used them as accelerators; they were withdrawn in 1996.
quick.mechanism: Psoralen enters skin and, when hit by UVA, binds DNA and triggers damage responses and pigment production.
quick.risks: Documented harms include severe phototoxic burns and skin loss after sunbathing with psoralen products. Long-term PUVA is associated with skin cancer including melanoma, and psoralens are described as photocarcinogenic.

chain: Psoralen absorbed or applied to skin
UVA exposure activates it and triggers melanocyte pigment production
Skin darkens faster; in vitiligo, pale patches repigment
angle.text: Under UVA light, psoralen stimulates pigment production, which is why it was added to tanning activators and why PUVA is used to repigment vitiligo patches. Its tanning use was discontinued in 1996 after photocarcinogenicity findings.
